title: A year of longing
hookLine: an old Punjabi form: twelve months, each colored by longing for the Beloved

lines: THE SEASONS POINT AT WHO ISN'T THERE.
cards: Being apart from someone you love changes the calendar. The first cold morning reminds you of their coat. A summer storm reminds you of the porch where you watched one together.
A festival comes, and there's an empty chair. The seasons keep pointing at who isn't there.

Folk singers in Punjab turned that feeling into a song form, already old, tradition says, when the Gurus took it up: a woman whose beloved is far away, singing her way through the year, one month at a time.

teach.b: It's called barah maha. Barah is twelve, maha is months. In the folk songs, each month has its weather and its work: the heat of one, the rains of another, the harvest, the festivals.
In each, the woman sings how the season sharpens her missing. The rain falls and he isn't here. The swings go up in the trees and he isn't here.
Two Gurus turned this folk form toward the One. Guru Nanak wrote a Barah Maha in Rag Tukhari, near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, wrote one in Rag Majh, on ang 133, and that's the one we'll walk through, month by month.
In Gurbani, the beloved far away isn't a husband off at war or trade. It's the One, and the woman singing is the soul.

That image, the soul as a bride longing for the divine Husband, runs all through the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs of every gender sing it as their own. The form's power is that it doesn't save longing for special days.
It finds it in the ordinary turn of the calendar. Each month has its own color of missing, so each month becomes a chance to remember.

teach.h: READ ON SANGRAND, MONTH BY MONTH.
teach.b: Gurdwaras that mark sangrand, the first day of the solar month, read that month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; some Sikhs keep the day and others don't.
Where it's kept, the calendar on the wall becomes a calendar of longing too.

games.q: you're Guru Arjan, and you know a folk song where a woman misses her husband through every season. what do you do with it?
o: leave it to the village singers.
turn it toward the One: the soul longing month by month.
replace it with a song about festivals.
games.why: Guru Arjan wrote a Barah Maha in Rag Majh: the soul as the bride, the One as the Beloved, each month its own longing.

practice: Ask what this month is like where you are, the light, the temperature, what's growing or dying, what the evenings smell like, and let one detail come clearly.

Then notice whether the month carries any longing, a person, a place, or an ache you can't quite name, and let the season and the longing sit together without fixing either. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Barah Maha. The twelve months: an old Punjabi song form where each season colors the longing for an absent beloved. In Gurbani, the Beloved is the One.
